description: We are a team of 5 IB and Non IB Physics students from Hawar International School in grades [11 and 12]. We joined the hackathon because we love applying what we learn in class, such as orbital motion, waves, radiation and mechanics, to real space problems.
summary:
Every six months, NASA’s SPHEREx telescope photographs the entire sky. Hidden in those pictures are things that move: brown dwarfs, fast stars, asteroids. Nobody has time to check them all. So we, The Hawar Space Odyssey, built SkyBlink, a free website where anyone can help look.

The trick is simple. Take two photos of the same patch of sky, taken months apart, and flip between them. The distant stars don’t budge, but anything close to us jumps. That’s exactly how Pluto was found in 1930, and you can learn it in about a minute.
SkyBlink starts you off with Sky Hunt, a game on a practice sky where you click whatever moves. Once you’ve got the hang of it, you move on to the Real Sky viewer, where you can pick any spot, change how you view it, check brightness and color charts, and save what you find in a logbook. There’s also an orbit explainer and a built-in guide for questions.

We wanted a curious twelve-year-old to be able to open it on a phone and start exploring, with nothing to install. The sky is too big for scientists alone, and more eyes mean more discoveries.
